content: Free oxygen radicals are believed to play a significant role in the development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) in preterm infants. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an enzyme that naturally occurs in the body and serves as a defense mechanism against oxidative damage. Clinical trials have been conducted to evaluate whether providing supplemental SOD can prevent BPD in preterm infants. The primary objective of this research was to assess the efficacy and safety of SOD in preventing and treating BPD, as well as its impact on mortality and other complications associated with prematurity in infants who are at risk for or already have BPD. To gather relevant studies, databases such as CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and three trial registries were searched on September 22, 2022. Additional studies were identified through reference checking, citation searching, and direct contact with study authors. The inclusion criteria were randomized, quasi-randomized, and cluster-randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving preterm infants who were either at risk of developing BPD or had already developed it. These infants were randomly assigned to receive SOD (in any form, dose, or route of administration) or a placebo/no treatment. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. The primary outcomes assessed included BPD defined as an oxygen requirement at 28 days, BPD defined as oxygen dependency at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, neonatal mortality, mortality prior to discharge, and a combined outcome of BPD or death at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age. Risk ratios (RR) and risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence for each outcome. Three RCTs involving a total of 380 preterm infants at risk for BPD were included in the analysis. No studies were identified that specifically focused on preterm infants with evolving BPD or early respiratory insufficiency. The evidence regarding the effect of SOD on BPD defined as an oxygen requirement at 28 days was highly uncertain (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.26; RD 0.06, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.16; 1 study, 302 infants). Similarly, the evidence was very uncertain for BPD defined as oxygen dependency at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.29; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.09; 2 studies, 335 infants). Neonatal mortality (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.68; RD -0.00, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.07; 2 studies, 335 infants) and mortality prior to discharge (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.71; RD 0.04, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.23; 2 studies, 78 infants) also showed very uncertain evidence. No studies reported on the combined outcome of BPD or death at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age. The effect of SOD on retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) at any stage was also highly uncertain (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.15; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.08; 2 studies, 335 infants). For severe ROP, the evidence remained very uncertain (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.65; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.09; 1 study, 244 infants). No studies reported on moderate to severe neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18 to 24 months of age. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low. Furthermore, no ongoing trials were identified. The most recent trial on SOD in preterm infants was conducted in 1997/1998, and no new studies have been initiated since then. In conclusion, the evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effects of SOD on BPD, neonatal mortality, mortality prior to discharge, and other complications such as ROP. No data are available on long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Given the limited and outdated evidence, further preclinical and observational studies are needed to provide a rationale for conducting new RCTs. Observational studies could also provide insights into the administration of SOD, including its indications, dosing, and associations with outcomes such as mortality, BPD, and long-term neurodevelopment.
